idea: Zipf's law of Moby-Dick: a program counts every word in the novel and plots rank against frequency on log-log axes, so thousands of tiny word-dots fall into an almost straight diagonal, with 'the' alone at the top. Caption: 'Rank × frequency ≈ constant.' It's for people who like the idea that a whole novel about obsession follows a hidden law.

A Voynich manuscript transition web: code takes the EVA transcription and draws every glyph as a node on a circle, with a curve for each time one glyph follows another, which makes a dense, lace-like rosette. Caption: 'Fluent. Still unread.' It's for anyone who loves a mystery the computers haven't cracked either.

The Rosetta Stone as three stacked ribbons: a program turns the hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek texts into three bands of stroke density, so you can see one message written three ways. Caption: 'Same decree, three times. 196 BC.' It's a smart nod to how a bilingual stone let people read hieroglyphs again.

The Linotype keyboard, drawn from its own logic: code lays out the machine's key rows, ordered by letter frequency, and sizes each key by how often that letter turns up in English. Caption: 'etaoin shrdlu'. Operators ran a finger down the first rows to fill a botched line, and that nonsense sometimes got printed in newspapers by mistake, so this is a typesetter's in-joke.

Enigma Rotor I: its real wiring (EKMFLGDQVZNTOWYHXUSPAIBRCJ) drawn as 26 chords crossing a circle of letters, a clean geometric star. Caption: 'No letter ever became itself.' Because of the reflector, Enigma could never encrypt a letter as itself, and that flaw helped the codebreakers at Bletchley Park.

The Morse alphabet sorted by length: a program stacks every letter's dots and dashes, from E (a single dot) down to the long codes, so the shape works like a frequency chart. Caption: 'E is one dot because printers had the most E's.' The story is that Alfred Vail counted the type in a printer's cases to decide which letters got the shortest codes.

All the type Gutenberg needed: code draws a grid of the roughly 290 different sorts (letters, ligatures and abbreviations) that were cut to set the 42-line Bible. Caption: '26 letters. About 290 pieces of metal.' It's for people who know that a 'simple' alphabet was a huge engineering job.

Absalom, Absalom! as a spiral: a program draws each sentence of Faulkner's novel as a stroke whose length matches its word count, and one sentence wraps around the whole shirt. Caption: 'One sentence: 1,288 words.' Guinness listed it in 1983 as the longest sentence in literature, which makes this a brag for maximalist readers.

A family tree for 'mother': code builds a branching tree from the reconstructed Proto-Indo-European root to its descendants (mātṛ, mḗtēr, mater, Mutter, mother, mat'), set in a fine monoline. Caption: '*méh₂tēr'. It shows that half the world is saying nearly the same first word.

The vowel space: a scatter of Peterson and Barney's 1952 formant measurements (F1 against F2), each cloud of dots labelled with its IPA vowel, so the plot forms the ghost of a mouth. Caption: 'Where your tongue goes.' It's real phonetics data that reads like a star chart.

Where lorem ipsum comes from: a program prints Cicero's real line 'Neque porro quisquam est qui dolorem ipsum quia dolor sit amet' and draws thin lines from it to the cut-up 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet' it became. Caption: 'Cicero, 45 BC. Scrambled for placeholders.' Designers know the filler text, and few know it was once philosophy about pain.

The finger path of one word: code traces the typing of 'typewriter' over a drawn QWERTY layout, and the line never leaves the top row. Caption: 'typewriter — top row only.' It's a small, true quirk of the keyboard, drawn as a precise little diagram.

'Call me Ishmael.' in Braille only: a program renders the line as a field of large six-dot cells, with the empty positions shown as faint rings, and a tiny note: 'Moby-Dick, line one.' It's a famous opening that you read by knowing the code, not by sight.

Pride and Prejudice with the words removed: code strips out every letter and keeps only the punctuation, in reading order, as a long texture of commas, semicolons and quotation marks. Caption: 'Austen, without the words.' Readers can feel her rhythm even with nothing left to read.

The Copiale cipher: a program redraws a page of its abstract symbols and roman letters, with a fine overlay line linking each symbol to its deciphered German letter. Caption: 'Secret society, 1730s. Decoded by computer, 2011.' Kevin Knight's team used statistical machine translation to crack the 105-page manuscript, which describes initiation rites.

One letter, a hundred typefaces: code overlays the lowercase 'a' from a hundred classic fonts at low opacity, and they build into one soft, ghostly average letter. Caption: 'a'. It's a quiet shirt for type nerds, about how many ways there are to agree on one shape.

Every way to break a paragraph: a program draws the Knuth–Plass graph for one paragraph, with a node for each possible line break and an arc for each line, and TeX's chosen path in solid ink through a haze of alternatives. Caption: 'TeX picks one.' It's for people who notice good justification and love the 1981 algorithm behind it.

The Phaistos Disc unwound: code reads both faces of the disc's stamped spiral and redraws it as one continuous line of glyphs, coloured by sign type. Caption: '45 signs. Stamped, not written. Never read.' The Bronze Age disc was printed with stamps, more than 3,000 years before Gutenberg, and nobody has deciphered it.

A dictionary eating itself: a program takes a public-domain dictionary and draws arrows from each headword to the words in its definition, which makes a dense, circular network. Caption: 'Every word is defined by other words.' It's a smart, slightly dizzying point about how language holds itself up.

Ulysses as a galaxy: code places every distinct word in Joyce's novel on a spiral, sizing each one by how often it appears, so a few giants sit among a huge dust of words used only once. Caption: 'Ulysses: about 30,000 different words.' It's for readers who finished it, or plan to.
